Separable treatment effects and tests given covariate values

Source: R/effects.R
aste.Rd

Estimates, for given covariate values \(x\), the separable treatment effects \(STE_{1,K}\) and \(STE_{2,K}\) on the two responses, the total treatment effect \(TTE_K\), the absolute separable treatment effects \(ASTE_{j,K} = |STE_{j,K}|\) and their difference \(DASTE_K = ASTE_{1,K} - ASTE_{2,K}\), with delta-method standard errors, and tests whether the treatment affects the second response more than the first (Section 3.2.1 of the paper).

Usage

aste(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  y1 = NULL,
  y2 = NULL,
  K = NULL,
  alternative = c("less", "greater", "two.sided"),
  conf.level = 0.95
)

Arguments

object

A fitted model returned by biscal().

newdata

A data frame of covariate values, one row per covariate profile \(x\) (for example, a row of the data, or the smallest or largest value of each covariate as in Table 2 of the paper). May be omitted when the model has no covariates.

y1, y2

Thresholds of the generalized odds ratio: categories of the first and second response (any category except the highest). Default to the lowest category, the only choice for binary responses.

K

End time point(s): the visit(s) at which the effects are defined. Defaults to the last visit of the data; a vector gives effects at several visits (see plot.biscal_aste()). Visits after the last visit of the data are extrapolated with the fitted transition models (with a warning).

alternative

Alternative hypothesis for the test of \(DASTE_K\) (\(DEASTE_K\) for easte()): "less" (default, as in the paper), "greater" or "two.sided".

conf.level

Confidence level of the Wald intervals.

Value

An object of class "biscal_aste", a list with components

effects

Data frame with one row per profile, end time and effect (STE1, STE2, TTE, ASTE1, ASTE2, DASTE): estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high.

test

Data frame with the test of \(DASTE_K\) for each profile and end time: estimate, std.error, statistic (\(z\)) and p.value.

gor

Data frame of the estimated generalized odds ratios of the four arms.

and the settings used.

Definitions

With \(GOR_K(a_1, a_2)\) the generalized odds ratio of the responses at the end time point \(K\) under treatment components \((a_1, a_2)\) (see gor()), $$TTE_K = \log\frac{GOR_K(1,1)}{GOR_K(0,0)},$$ $$STE_{1,K} = \log\frac{GOR_K(1,1)}{GOR_K(0,1)} + \log\frac{GOR_K(1,0)}{GOR_K(0,0)},$$ $$STE_{2,K} = \log\frac{GOR_K(1,1)}{GOR_K(1,0)} + \log\frac{GOR_K(0,1)}{GOR_K(0,0)},$$ so that \(STE_{1,K} + STE_{2,K} = 2\,TTE_K\) (Theorem 1 of the paper). \(STE_{1,K}\) changes the treatment component acting on the first response with the other component held fixed, and \(STE_{2,K}\) conversely.

Inference

Standard errors use the delta method with the covariance matrix of the maximum likelihood estimators (equation (24) of the paper); the derivatives are central differences with step \(\epsilon^{1/3}\) (\(\epsilon\) the machine precision), as in the authors' implementation, and the absolute values are differentiated through \(\mathrm{sign}(STE_{j,K})\), a subgradient. The default test is that of the paper, \(H_0: DASTE_K \ge 0\) against \(H_1: DASTE_K < 0\) (the absolute separable effect on the second response is larger), with p-value \(\Phi(z)\), \(z = \widehat{DASTE}_K / \widehat{se}\). Confidence intervals are Wald intervals.

References

Hu, P. and Yi, G. Y. (2026). Inference about separable causal effects with longitudinal bivariate ordinal responses with missingness and censoring. Statistics in Medicine, 45, e70320. doi:10.1002/sim.70320

See also

easte() for the population-level effects; gor(); plot.biscal_aste().

Examples

fit <- biscal(cbind(y1, y2) ~ x1 + x2, data = simtrial, id = "id",
              time = "visit", treatment = "trt")
# effects for two covariate profiles
profiles <- data.frame(x1 = c(-1, 1), x2 = c(0, 1))
res <- aste(fit, newdata = profiles)
res
#> Separable treatment effects given covariate values (individual level)
#> Thresholds: y1 <= 0, y2 <= 0; Wald 95% confidence intervals
#> 
#> Profile 1 (x1 = -1, x2 = 0), end time K = 10:
#>       Estimate Std. Error Lower 95% Upper 95%
#> STE1  -0.07897    0.02238   -0.1228  -0.03509
#> STE2  -0.03184    0.01304  -0.05739 -0.006276
#> TTE   -0.05540    0.01037  -0.07572  -0.03508
#> ASTE1  0.07897    0.02238   0.03509    0.1228
#> ASTE2  0.03184    0.01304  0.006276   0.05739
#> DASTE  0.04713    0.03021  -0.01207    0.1063
#> H0: DASTE >= 0 vs H1: DASTE < 0: z = 1.560, p-value = 0.941
#> 
#> Profile 2 (x1 = 1, x2 = 1), end time K = 10:
#>       Estimate Std. Error Lower 95% Upper 95%
#> STE1  -0.06218    0.02425   -0.1097  -0.01466

#> DASTE 0.007958    0.03947  -0.06940   0.08532
#> H0: DASTE >= 0 vs H1: DASTE < 0: z = 0.2016, p-value = 0.58
as.data.frame(res)
